clue.text: In one sense weight is a test of gold

parts.note: touch is one of the five senses
a stone is a British weight of fourteen pounds

explanation.surface: A remark about how gold is assayed, where one method relies on weighing it.
explanation.walkthrough: A touchstone was a dark stone on which gold was rubbed so the streak showed its purity. STONE is a British unit of weight, 14 pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: The original touchstone was a black siliceous stone used to assay precious metal by the colour of its streak.

clue.text: Drink money, duck ?

parts.note: tea is a drink
L stands for the pound (libra), British money

explanation.surface: Someone asked to buy a round, or to dodge paying for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'duck' looks like a verb (to dodge), but it is the bird. L is the sign for the pound sterling.
explanation.definitionFit: The teal is a small freshwater dabbling bird of the family Anatidae.

clue.text: Aunt Olive shows the direction

indicators.note: the word appears within Aunt Olive, as if displayed there

explanation.surface: An elderly relative pointing the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shows' signals letters inside 'Aunt Olive'. The archaic preposition means towards, a direction.
explanation.definitionFit: The old preposition means to or towards, marking direction of movement.

clue.text: Common loaves about 25 cents at the depot

indicators.note: the heads surround the coin, so they are put about it

parts.note: in common slang a loaf (of bread) is the head, so loaves are heads
a quarter is the American 25-cent coin

explanation.surface: Ordinary bread costing a quarter at the supply store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Use your loaf' is British slang from rhyming slang 'loaf of bread' for head. 'about' puts HEADS around QUARTER.
explanation.definitionFit: A regimental depot serves as the headquarters of a military unit.

clue.text: It was included in the Church's perquisites

definitions.note: plural in the clue, while the answer is one tenth-part payment; the levy collectively makes up the church's dues

indicators.note: the first word goes inside the article that follows it

explanation.surface: Something was part of the clergy's perks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'was included in' places IT inside THE.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenth of produce or income was due to support the parish priest, his traditional entitlement.

clue.text: Refusal to corrupt an apprentice

parts.note: no is a refusal
to vitiate is to spoil or corrupt

explanation.surface: A trainee's refusal to be corrupted.
explanation.walkthrough: VITIATE means to impair or corrupt.
explanation.definitionFit: A novitiate can mean a novice, a beginner on probation in a religious order.

clue.text: Old Harrovians keeping their distance after forty years

definitions.text: Old Harrovians keeping their distance after forty years

parts.words: Old Harrovians keeping their distance after forty years
parts.note: the Harrow School song 'Forty Years On' pictures old boys, decades later, scattered far from one another

explanation.surface: Former pupils of Harrow School drifting apart in middle age.
explanation.walkthrough: Harrow is an English public school whose song 'Forty Years On' begins 'Forty years on, when afar and asunder / Parted are those who are singing today'. The clue quotes the word that describes the old boys' separation.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means at a great distance, the word the Harrow school song uses for old boys long parted.

clue.text: This palace gives highest honour — to one so unpopular ?

definitions.text: This palace gives highest honour — to one so unpopular ?

parts.words: This palace gives highest honour — to one so unpopular
parts.note: the word palace split as pal plus ace: someone without a pal leaves only the ace, the top honour in cards

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'palace' as PAL + ACE. For someone with no pal, 'palace' loses PAL and gives ACE, the highest honour in a card suit. Having no pal is having no companion.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with no pal has no companions at all, which is the lonely state described.

clue.text: The state of a borough in the state of Denmark ?

definitions.meaning: the condition of a rotten borough, a parliamentary seat with almost no voters before 1832
Hamlet's 'something is rotten in the state of Denmark' names the decay there

explanation.walkthrough: Rotten boroughs were British constituencies with tiny electorates, abolished by the 1832 Reform Act.
explanation.definitionFit: A corrupt pre-1832 seat was a 'rotten borough', and Marcellus says 'Something is rotten in the state of Denmark' in Hamlet, so both describe decay.

clue.text: "Here's metal more" (Hamlet)

parts.note: a gap-fill: the missing word completes Hamlet's line at the play scene, said as he turns to Ophelia

explanation.walkthrough: In Act 3 Scene 2 Hamlet declines his mother's seat beside her with 'No, good mother, here's metal more ...', meaning Ophelia draws him more strongly, like a magnet drawing iron.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet means Ophelia is a stronger magnet for him, so the missing word describes something that pulls or draws.

clue.text: The point of a non-Civvy Street in the US

parts.note: someone who is not a civilian is a soldier, and in America a soldier is a GI

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about what a military road in America is for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Civvy Street' is British slang for civilian life, so 'non-Civvy Street' looks like one phrase meaning the forces; it splits into a soldier (GI, as 'in the US' says) and ST for Street.
explanation.definitionFit: The main thrust or essence of an argument is its gist.

clue.text: Sidney upset over his entering the country — how to stop his crossing?

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits over the rest
in a down clue upset turns the short name upwards, back to front

parts.note: Sid is the short form of Sidney

indicators.note: the possessive goes inside the country's name

parts.note: France is the country
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man named Sidney is upset at another man entering the country, and wonders how to stop him crossing the border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns SID into DIS; 'entering' puts HIS inside FRANCE. 'his crossing' is the X he marks on a ballot paper, not crossing a border.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking away someone's right to vote stops him putting his cross on a ballot paper.

clue.text: Queen's entire embarrassment caused by Lady Godiva?

indicators.note: embarrassment throws everything into confusion, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: the apostrophe is ignored and all six letters are used
taken as written

explanation.surface: The monarch is mortified by the naked ride of Lady Godiva.
explanation.walkthrough: 'embarrassment' jumbles QUEENS and ENTIRE together. Lady Godiva, by legend, rode naked on horseback through Coventry, so the question mark marks her as an example of a horsewoman.
explanation.definitionFit: Godiva's famous ride makes her an example of a female horse rider.

clue.text: He does no good to your image

definitions.text: He does no good to your image

parts.words: He does no good to your image
parts.note: one who harms your reputation, read literally as one who smashes your religious statue

explanation.walkthrough: 'image' suggests public reputation, but here it is a sacred image: the man destroys icons.
explanation.definitionFit: Originally a destroyer of religious images, the word now means an attacker of cherished beliefs.

clue.text: Get in a grim mess ? Here's one way out

indicators.note: making a mess of the letters puts them in disorder

explanation.surface: Someone in trouble finds a means of escape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mess' jumbles GET IN A GRIM. Leaving your country is one way out of a bad situation.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving abroad permanently is a way of leaving one's homeland behind.

clue.text: Flower girl out of the North follows the river

indicators.note: the girl's part comes after the river's part, so it follows it in the answer

parts.note: the Cam is the river through Cambridge

indicators.note: the girl's name sits outside the letter for North, wrapping it

parts.note: Paula is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A flower girl who has left the north of the country goes along a riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower girl' looks like one phrase, but Flower is the definition. 'out of' puts PAULA around N, giving PANULA, and 'follows' places it after CAM, the Cambridge river.
explanation.definitionFit: Campanula is the bellflower genus, a garden plant with bell-shaped blooms.

clue.text: Like Julius Caesar after three refusals

definitions.text: Like Julius Caesar after three refusals

parts.words: Like Julius Caesar after three refusals
parts.note: Mark Antony says he thrice offered Caesar a kingly crown, which he thrice refused, so he stayed a ruler without one

explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's 'Julius Caesar', Antony recalls 'I thrice presented him a kingly crown, Which he did thrice refuse'.
explanation.definitionFit: Having refused the kingly diadem, Caesar remained a ruler never formally made king.

clue.text: Look in the marsh for a criminal

indicators.note: the exclamation is placed within the word for wetland

parts.note: a fen is a low marshy area
lo is an old word for look, as in 'lo and behold'

explanation.surface: Searching a swamp for an escaped convict.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a manhunt; in fact 'in' puts LO inside FEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A felon is someone who has committed a serious crime.

clue.text: One from MI

parts.note: MI is the Roman numeral 1001, recalling the Thousand and One tales of Scheherazade

explanation.walkthrough: MI looks like British intelligence (MI5), but read it as Roman numerals: 1001, as in 'The Thousand and One Nights', so one of them is a single evening of tales.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arabian tales are counted by evenings, so one of the thousand and one is a single evening.

clue.text: Mountain hazards for round about 105 beasts of burden

indicators.note: the Roman numeral goes round the short word for about

parts.note: in Roman numerals C is 100 and V is 5
re means about or concerning
asses are donkeys used to carry loads

explanation.surface: Mountain dangers facing a pack train of about a hundred and five donkeys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' puts CV (Roman 105) around RE (about), giving CREV, before ASSES.
explanation.definitionFit: Deep cracks in glaciers are a classic danger to climbers.

clue.text: Sight of the unseen

parts.note: the power of seeing what is hidden from ordinary eyes, the gift claimed by a psychic

explanation.walkthrough: The paradox of seeing what cannot be seen points to second sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Second sight is the supposed faculty of perceiving things beyond the normal senses.

clue.text: Legitimate to be beheaded — but terrible

indicators.note: losing the head means the first letter is cut off

parts.note: lawful means legitimate

explanation.surface: A lawful execution that is still horrifying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be beheaded' removes the first letter of LAWFUL.
explanation.definitionFit: Awful is a common synonym of dreadful or very bad.

clue.text: Ancient Greek's price for a talking bird ?

definitions.meaning: a sum of money in ancient Greece, a coin weight of a hundred drachmas
the Asian starling famous for imitating speech, in one of its spellings

explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks what a Greek would pay for a parrot-like bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Greek mina was a unit of weight and money worth 100 drachmas; the same spelling is a variant of myna, the mimicking starling.

clue.text: Lack of gravity would make such mirth general

parts.note: G is the symbol for gravity
Robert E. Lee was the Confederate general

explanation.surface: A complaint that solemn people make merriment too widespread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lack of gravity' means drop G from the answer, which then leaves a general, LEE, the American Civil War commander; so the answer is G + LEE. 'general' looks like an adjective (widespread) but is the soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: Glee is joyful merriment.

clue.text: World revolutionary centre

parts.note: the line about which a planet spins, read instead as the headquarters of global revolution

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a hub of political revolutionaries, but 'revolutionary' means turning: the Earth rotates about an imaginary line.
explanation.definitionFit: The Earth spins about the imaginary line through its poles.

clue.text: "An English rose" (Brooke)

parts.note: a gap-fill: the missing word completes a line of Rupert Brooke's poem 'Grantchester'

explanation.walkthrough: In 'Grantchester' Rupert Brooke, homesick in Berlin, sets German tulips against 'An unofficial English rose', a wild rose growing unplanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Brooke's wild rose is not formally planted or sanctioned, hence not authorised.

clue.text: In which to gad about in Rome

definitions.text: In which to gad about in Rome

indicators.note: the opening word says the garment is contained within the next words of the clue

explanation.surface: A garment for strolling around ancient Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' signals letters inside 'to gad'; the whole clue then describes the Roman garment one would wear while going about the city.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman citizen's loose outer robe was the usual dress for going about the city.

clue.text: Mature eater is distressed if you so treat his food

definitions.text: if you so treat his food

parts.note: grown up, as an adult is

indicators.note: being distressed, the word eater is put into disorder

explanation.surface: A grown-up diner would be upset if his meal were tampered with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is distressed' jumbles EATER into ERATE after ADULT. The definition reads 'if you so treat (adulterate) his food'.
explanation.definitionFit: To contaminate food by mixing in an inferior substance is the treatment meant.
